realization_factors.factor_id: Certified third-party EPC installation and Bloom consult-only execution
realization_factors.condition: Each committed Energy Server site has a qualified installer and an unambiguous responsibility model for equipment installation, site construction, electrical and gas integration, commissioning, and handover, without a scope or quality gap between the EPC, customer, and Bloom.
realization_factors.current_status: Bloom is shifting large-load sites toward customers contracting directly with certified third-party EPCs while Bloom provides product consulting. The Q2 filing describes a training and qualification program based on product and infrastructure experience, balance sheet, reputation, and safety record. This establishes an execution mechanism rather than repeatable project proof: Q2 installation gross margin was approximately -4%, and project-level EPC throughput, rework, commissioning, and acceptance cadence are not disclosed.
realization_factors.impact: This is the field handoff through which a committed unit becomes an installed and commissioned system. A qualified EPC can reduce Bloom's direct labor and installation-cost burden, but weak capacity, scope control, or rework can delay acceptance, shift customer-interface and guarantee costs back to Bloom, and reduce project net economics.

observability.match_condition: Future project disclosures or filings identify the responsibility model, certified EPC selection and capacity, construction start and completion, commissioning, rework or claims, customer handover, and installation margin and cash outcomes by delivery model.

realization_factors.factor_id: Committed-site permitting, interconnection, and fuel-readiness gate
realization_factors.condition: A committed site obtains the air, environmental, construction, electrical and gas interconnection, and fuel-infrastructure approvals needed to install, energize, commission, and accept the Energy Server on schedule.
realization_factors.current_status: Permitting and interconnection remain external gates even after a project is treated as committed. On 2026-09-17 the New Mexico Supreme Court allowed the Project Jupiter permitting process to resume, but the hearing officer and schedule still had to be reset; Bloom's Q2 filing also warns that community opposition and permits can lengthen sales and installation cycles. No project-level clearance-to-commissioning cadence was available at the cutoff.
realization_factors.impact: Without site approvals, interconnection, or fuel readiness, the EPC cannot complete field work or energize the system for acceptance. A delay pushes revenue and cash use, can strand inventory or create rework, and can expose the project to cancellation or changed scope; the adjacent project-feasibility shell owns the full regulatory system, while this factor tracks its post-commitment field consequence.

observability.match_condition: A future project update records permit issuance or suspension, electrical or gas interconnection approval, fuel-infrastructure status, construction start, commissioning date, hearing or challenge outcome, and any associated delay, cancellation, or scope change.

realization_factors.condition: Installed Energy Server systems pass commissioning and performance tests and receive customer acceptance on the planned milestone schedule.
realization_factors.current_status: Q2 product and total revenue were strong, but reported revenue, framework capacity, and nominal production plans do not establish accepted MW. The filing attributes working-capital movements to milestone billings and customer-acceptance cycles, while project-level customer sign-offs, acceptance cadence, and post-commissioning performance evidence remain undisclosed; the current acceptance anchor is therefore mixed and weak.
realization_factors.impact: Acceptance is the gate that completes handover and releases the intended billing and contract-asset conversion. Delayed or failed tests leave equipment, deferred costs, and contract assets outstanding, extend cash usage, and can create liquidated-damage, rework, or warranty exposure even when the system has shipped or revenue has been reported.

observability.match_condition: Future filings, customer announcements, or project records show MW delivered, commissioning completion, customer sign-off, acceptance-to-cash lag, contract-asset reduction, deferred-cost release, performance-test results, and cancellations or acceptance disputes.

realization_factors.factor_id: Project installation cost and working-capital conversion
realization_factors.condition: For each delivery responsibility model, project billing, deposits, contract assets, inventory, vendor payments, and EPC or installation costs convert accepted delivery into controlled net economics and cash use.
realization_factors.current_status: Direct purchase represented 99% of Q2 revenue and installation gross margin was approximately -4%. H1 operating cash flow was $300.0 million, but accounts receivable and contract assets increased $276.7 million, customer deposits increased $226.2 million, inventory increased $115.1 million, and a $247.6 million vendor-payment timing benefit supported cash; no project-level cost and cash bridge is disclosed.
realization_factors.impact: This mechanism changes the magnitude, timing, and beneficiary of delivery economics rather than whether a unit can physically be installed. Consult-only EPC may lower Bloom's direct cost and installation revenue together; delayed acceptance or inventory build can consume cash, while deposits and vendor timing can temporarily mask weak project conversion.

observability.match_condition: Subsequent reporting provides project-level revenue, EPC and Bloom cost scope, installation margin, deposits, contract-asset-to-cash conversion, inventory consumption, vendor-payment terms, and cash usage per accepted project.

realization_factors.condition: Power Connect's pre-connected and factory-tested electrical integration reduces site installation and commissioning time without increasing defects, rework, or downstream acceptance failures.
realization_factors.current_status: Bloom introduced Power Connect on 2026-08-19 and described a minimum three-month on-site deployment and potential installation-time reduction above 40%. At the cutoff this was a product and management claim; no accepted-project comparison of installation hours, commissioning failures, or rework was available.
realization_factors.impact: If repeatable, factory integration can shorten the field cycle, reduce site labor and integration risk, and improve project cash timing. If not, errors can move from site installation into factory or commissioning rework; it does not by itself prove EPC capacity, permit readiness, or customer acceptance.

observability.match_condition: Future Power Connect project disclosures compare factory-integrated and conventional deployments on installation duration, commissioning defects, rework, field cost, acceptance timing, and post-handover incidents.

realization_factors.factor_id: Energy Server warranty and performance-guarantee cost containment
realization_factors.condition: Repairs, replacements, warranty claims, and performance-guarantee payments on delivered Energy Server systems remain bounded relative to project economics after acceptance.
realization_factors.current_status: The Q2 filing reports no liabilities from failure to repair or replace systems under the O&M performance warranties, but aggregate performance-guarantee caps were approximately $846.1 million and remaining potential exposure was approximately $468.9 million at June 30, 2026; payments were $5.4 million in Q2 and $13.8 million in H1. A project-vintage loss and replacement curve is not disclosed, so exposure is not treated as a forecast of realized loss.
realization_factors.impact: Post-acceptance performance obligations can reverse otherwise acceptable project economics through replacement, repair, credits, or cash payments. The burden mainly changes margin and cash conversion, but persistent low output or low efficiency can also delay acceptance, weaken customer references, and shift future responsibility-model choices.

observability.match_condition: Future filings or service disclosures show warranty accruals, repair and replacement events, performance claims and payments by project or fleet vintage, remaining guarantee exposure, and net installation or project economics after those obligations.

potential_gaps.gap_id: Multi-site certified-EPC delivery validates consult-only execution
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: Two or more subsequent large-load Energy Server projects use named certified third-party EPCs with Bloom consult-only support, reach commissioning and customer handover within their planned windows, and disclose no material scope dispute or rework.
potential_gaps.derivation: Bloom is moving later large-load projects toward customer-contracted certified EPCs while retaining a consult-only role, and its qualification program is described by experience, balance sheet, reputation, and safety criteria. The current record establishes an intended mechanism but not repeatable project proof; a multi-site rollout that closes the installation-to-handover loop therefore remains a material upside path.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Upgrade the proposition's support for schedule and controlled installation and treat the third-party model as a demonstrated scalable execution path. Do not infer positive project net economics or cash conversion unless the same evidence reports project costs, acceptance timing, and cash outcomes.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: Project disclosures identify the EPC and responsibility scope, construction and commissioning dates, and customer handover for multiple later projects, with no material unresolved rework, claims, or schedule variance.

potential_gaps.gap_id: Certified-EPC capacity or scope failure delays committed sites
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: A committed large-load site misses installation or commissioning because its certified EPC cannot staff or sequence the work, or leaves electrical, gas, or handoff scope unresolved; Bloom or the customer takes back material work.
potential_gaps.derivation: The consult-only transition moves field capacity and interface control to third parties while project-level EPC throughput, rework, and acceptance cadence remain undisclosed. A qualified-installer label may therefore fail to provide peak capacity or a complete scope, especially as large projects scale and Bloom still carries customer-facing obligations.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Downgrade the assumption that certified third-party EPC and consult-only execution can scale on schedule; move the horizon later and increase expected installation cost, Bloom support burden, acceptance risk, and project cash usage. A single EPC failure need not invalidate every delivery model, but it would weaken the scalable-model proposition until capacity and scope controls are demonstrated.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: A project update or filing records a milestone miss attributable to EPC capacity or interface scope, an EPC replacement or responsibility transfer, material rework, or a customer/Bloom claim before commissioning or handover.

potential_gaps.gap_id: Post-commitment permit-interconnection-fuel gate stalls commissioning
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: After a project is treated as committed, a permit, electrical interconnection, or fuel-infrastructure challenge suspends field work or prevents energization, producing a material commissioning delay, scope reduction, or cancellation.
potential_gaps.derivation: Project Jupiter's air-permit process was allowed to resume only after a court-related pause, with a new hearing officer and schedule still required, while the related gas pipeline has its own environmental review. Bloom's filing also identifies community opposition and permits as causes of longer installation cycles. A commitment can therefore encounter a later field-readiness blocker even when demand and equipment are available.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Delay the expected installation, energization, and acceptance horizon and lower confidence that committed capacity becomes accepted MW on schedule. Revise project cash usage and cancellation or scope-change risk upward; permit-system ownership remains with the adjacent project-feasibility shell, while this Unit records the post-commitment field consequence.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: A named committed project records a permit suspension or denial, interconnection or fuel-readiness failure, a reset construction or commissioning date, a material scope reduction, or cancellation tied to that gate.

potential_gaps.gap_id: New reliability or environmental requirements force field redesign
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: A regulator, utility, or customer imposes new computational-load reliability, air-quality, emissions, water, or fuel-network requirements that require a committed Energy Server microgrid to add controls or equipment or change its operating configuration before acceptance.
potential_gaps.derivation: NERC and FERC processes are developing reliability and registration requirements for computational loads, while Project Jupiter links fuel-cell operation to air, water, emissions, and gas-infrastructure reviews. These rules or conditions could change the field design after commercial commitment rather than simply delay an existing permit, creating an outside-model redesign path.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Revise the Unit to include a longer or staged commissioning path and higher site-specific installation and compliance cost. A regulatory qualification or revised design would not prove customer acceptance, margin, or cash conversion; those remain separate evidence requirements.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: A utility, regulator, customer, or EPC change order identifies a new reliability, environmental, emissions, water, or fuel-network requirement and the project plan shows added equipment, operating restrictions, redesign, or a changed acceptance date.

potential_gaps.gap_id: Balance-of-plant component shortage disrupts site sequence
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: A committed site cannot obtain a transformer, switchgear, gas-infrastructure component, or other balance-of-plant item on the planned schedule and must resequence, substitute, or pause field installation.
potential_gaps.derivation: Data-center power projects depend on long-lead grid and gas interfaces in addition to Bloom equipment. The event library records substation-transformer lead times above 160 weeks, and Bloom's own delivery evidence distinguishes nominal production from site-ready acceptance. A field component bottleneck can therefore migrate the constraint from manufacturing to installation without being a Bloom factory shortfall.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Push the delivery and acceptance horizon later and increase installation cash usage, temporary-equipment cost, and inventory or work-in-process risk. Do not treat the event as evidence that Bloom manufacturing throughput failed; it would identify a separate field-side bottleneck.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: A project record or filing explicitly links a construction or commissioning delay, substitution, or temporary-power arrangement to a transformer, switchgear, gas, or other balance-of-plant component shortage.

potential_gaps.gap_id: Commissioning test failure delays customer acceptance
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: One or more installed Energy Server sites fail output, efficiency, synchronization, safety, or integrated-microgrid performance tests, and customer acceptance is deferred or disputed.
potential_gaps.derivation: Current reported revenue, framework capacity, and nominal production plans do not establish accepted MW; the filing instead points to milestone billings and customer-acceptance cycles, with project-level sign-offs and performance-test results undisclosed. The disclosed performance-guarantee obligations provide a mechanism through which an installed system can still fail the final handover test.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Lower support for on-schedule acceptance and extend the delivery-to-cash cycle; increase rework, liquidated-damage, warranty, and contract-asset risk. Passing commissioning at another site would not remove the need for a project-specific acceptance record.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: A customer, EPC, filing, or project record documents a failed or repeated performance test, withheld sign-off, formal acceptance dispute, liquidated-damage claim, or contract-asset delay attributable to commissioning performance.

potential_gaps.gap_id: Partial customer acceptance reduces committed scope
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: A customer energizes or accepts only a portion of a committed Energy Server deployment and defers, resizes, or cancels the remaining units after initial installation or testing.
potential_gaps.derivation: Large framework capacities and announced projects are not accepted MW, and current evidence does not disclose customer-level cancellation rights, phased schedules, or acceptance cadence. Customer load timing, financing, or site readiness can therefore create a beneficiary and magnitude change after Bloom has begun field delivery.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Reduce the expected accepted MW and project-level revenue or move the completion horizon later, with unused inventory and field cash exposure potentially remaining. Partial acceptance would establish some delivery capability but would not validate the full committed project scope or repeatability across customers.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: A customer announcement, change order, filing, or project record distinguishes accepted or energized units from the remaining committed scope and records a deferral, resize, cancellation, or revised completion window for the balance.

potential_gaps.gap_id: Acceptance-to-cash conversion breaks after physical handover
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: A customer accepts or energizes a delivered system but milestone receivables or contract assets remain unpaid or are renegotiated beyond the planned cycle, requiring extended Bloom working capital or a loss provision.
potential_gaps.derivation: H1 operating cash flow benefited from customer deposits and vendor-payment timing while accounts receivable and contract assets also increased; management identifies acceptance cycles as a cash driver, but no project-level acceptance-to-cash bridge or customer credit outcomes is disclosed. Physical completion can therefore succeed while delivery-cycle cash conversion fails.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Keep the physical-delivery proposition separate from cash realization but downgrade controlled project cash usage and extend the working-capital horizon. A reported revenue or customer sign-off would not be treated as proof of cash conversion until the receivable or contract asset is collected on the expected terms.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: A project has documented customer acceptance or energization and the related receivable or contract asset persists across a subsequent reporting cycle, is placed in dispute/default status, receives materially extended terms, or generates a loss provision.

potential_gaps.gap_id: Consult-only transition fails to improve project net economics
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: Large-load projects delivered through certified EPC and consult-only arrangements show lower project contribution after Bloom support, engineering, warranty, guarantee, or customer/EPC pricing costs than comparable full-scope work.
potential_gaps.derivation: Q2 installation gross margin was approximately negative 4%, and the research explicitly notes that consult-only execution may reduce both Bloom's installation revenue and its direct cost. Without a project-level bridge, externalizing construction can transfer cost, interface, and guarantee obligations rather than improve net economics.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Downgrade the proposition's project-level economic control even if sites are installed on time, and revise the expected beneficiary and margin allocation between Bloom, the EPC, and the customer. Do not use lower reported installation revenue alone as evidence of improved economics.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: Project-level reporting for consult-only work identifies Bloom support and guarantee costs and shows net contribution below comparable full-scope projects or below zero after the relevant field obligations.

potential_gaps.gap_id: Accepted project cohort proves positive net economics and cash conversion
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: A disclosed cohort of accepted Energy Server projects across the material delivery models shows positive project contribution after Bloom, EPC, and customer installation scope, warranty, and field costs, and converts deposits or contract assets to cash within the planned cycle.
potential_gaps.derivation: The current shell has strong revenue and direct-purchase evidence but only weak project-level net-economics evidence; installation is loss-making in Q2 and working-capital movements are not tied to accepted projects. A cohort reconciliation would supply the missing link between acceptance, cost responsibility, and cash rather than relying on aggregate corporate results.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Upgrade support for controlled project-level net economics and delivery-cycle cash conversion, and narrow the current uncertainty around which party captures value. The result would not prove aggregate corporate earnings, manufacturing economics, or financing capacity outside this shell.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: A filing or customer/project disclosure reconciles accepted units or MW with project revenue, Bloom/EPC/customer cost scope, warranty or guarantee cost, deposits or contract assets, and subsequent cash collection for a defined cohort.

potential_gaps.gap_id: Power Connect validates field-cycle reduction
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: Commercial Power Connect deployments show a repeatable reduction in installation or commissioning duration relative to conventional electrical integration without higher defect, rework, or acceptance-failure rates.
potential_gaps.derivation: Power Connect moves key electrical integration into a pre-connected, factory-tested system and Bloom describes a minimum three-month on-site deployment with potential installation-time reduction above 40%, but no accepted-project comparison was available at the cutoff. Repeated field evidence could make the product a real modifier of schedule, cost, and cash timing.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Upgrade the Power Connect realization factor and shorten the expected field cycle or reduce site-integration risk within the projects that use it. It would not by itself prove permits, EPC capacity, customer acceptance, or positive project net economics.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: Multiple commercial Power Connect projects report comparable installation and commissioning durations against conventional integration, with actual defect, rework, and acceptance outcomes showing no material deterioration.

potential_gaps.gap_id: Power Connect integration defects create rework
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: Power Connect deployments produce recurring factory-to-site interface defects or integration rework that lengthen commissioning or create customer acceptance claims.
potential_gaps.derivation: Factory integration can move electrical complexity from the site into factory testing, logistics, and the final interface rather than eliminate it. Because Power Connect was newly introduced and the current evidence is a management deployment-time claim rather than an accepted-project series, a negative learning curve remains possible.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Downgrade Power Connect as a schedule and cost modifier, extend commissioning and cash-use expectations for affected sites, and increase warranty or acceptance risk. The revision would be limited to deployments using the integrated system unless the defect pattern is shown to be platform-wide.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: Two or more Power Connect project records identify a recurring integration defect, factory correction, field change order, rework episode, or acceptance delay attributable to the product's factory-to-site interface.

potential_gaps.gap_id: Early-life warranty cluster changes delivery economics
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: A recent Energy Server delivery cohort develops a material cluster of low-output, repair, replacement, or performance-guarantee claims after customer acceptance.
potential_gaps.derivation: The Q2 filing reports performance-guarantee payments of $5.4 million in the quarter and $13.8 million in H1, with approximately $468.9 million of potential remaining exposure, but no project-vintage loss or replacement curve. A new-vintage cluster would connect acceptance to a later reversal of project economics and could change which delivery responsibility model Bloom is willing to support.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Reduce confidence that accepted projects retain controlled net economics after handover, increase expected warranty and guarantee cost, and revise future delivery-model selection or pricing. Acceptance would still have occurred; the revision concerns post-acceptance field economics rather than the acceptance gate itself.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: A filing or service disclosure links a material increase in claims, payments, accruals, repairs, or replacements to a recent delivered project cohort or vintage rather than to an unrelated legacy population.

realization_factors.condition: The installed Energy Server fleet maintains contracted availability and output or efficiency as units age, with degradation and downtime inside the assumptions supporting O&M service economics.
realization_factors.current_status: Q2 service revenue was $69.0 million, up 26.8% year over year, and service gross margin was approximately 19%, but fleet-level availability, output, efficiency, degradation, and forced-outage series are not disclosed. Performance-guarantee payments show that some underperformance is economically active; the current fleet condition remains mixed with only moderate evidence.
realization_factors.impact: Availability and degradation determine whether a growing fleet produces dependable service revenue or creates outages, credits, repairs, replacements, and customer-renewal risk. A single successful or reported operating quarter does not establish a repeatable aging curve; deterioration can erode both service margin and the value of the installed base.

observability.match_condition: Future service disclosures report fleet MW and age cohorts, availability, output and efficiency, degradation, downtime, forced outages, stack or system replacements, and the effect on service revenue, margin, and customer claims.

realization_factors.factor_id: O&M contract retention and service-revenue capture
realization_factors.condition: A growing installed fleet remains covered by renewable O&M or service contracts whose scope, pricing, and renewal terms convert reliable operation into recurring service revenue.
realization_factors.current_status: Bloom attributes Q2 service growth to an expanding maintenance-contract fleet, consistent with $69.0 million of service revenue and 26.8% year-over-year growth. However, installed MW under contract, renewal and churn rates, pricing escalators, contract duration, and service revenue per MW are not disclosed; future service revenue is explicitly subject to performance-guarantee obligations.
realization_factors.impact: The installed fleet only becomes durable service profitability when service rights are retained and priced to cover labor, parts, replacements, and guarantees. Non-renewal, customer self-maintenance, weak pricing, or contract scope leakage can leave Bloom with field obligations and fixed service resources without the expected recurring revenue.

observability.match_condition: Future filings disclose installed MW under O&M, renewal and churn outcomes, contract duration and escalators, service revenue per MW, customer self-maintenance or termination, and gross margin after guarantee and replacement costs.

realization_factors.factor_id: Field maintenance, parts, and replacement execution
realization_factors.condition: Bloom and its service partners can procure parts and perform preventive and corrective maintenance and stack or system replacements fast enough to restore availability without service-cost overruns.
realization_factors.current_status: The Q2 filing records $132.3 million of prepaid and other current-asset growth, including upfront service-related payments aligned with expanding field-service activity, but it does not disclose fleet-level mean time to repair, parts lead times, replacement cadence, technician capacity, or post-repair availability. The service network is therefore a material but incompletely evidenced execution gate.
realization_factors.impact: Maintenance and replacement execution is the bridge from physical degradation to restored output. Parts or technician bottlenecks extend downtime and trigger guarantee payments; inefficient field work raises service cost and cash use even when service revenue grows, while repeatable repair cycles can preserve availability and margin.

observability.match_condition: Future operating data show preventive and corrective work orders, mean time to repair, parts availability and lead times, replacement rates and cost per MW, technician or partner capacity, backlog, and availability after repair.

realization_factors.factor_id: Energy Server warranty and performance-guarantee cost containment
realization_factors.condition: Repairs, replacements, warranty claims, and performance-guarantee payments on the installed fleet remain bounded relative to recurring O&M revenue and service gross margin.
realization_factors.current_status: The Q2 filing reports no liabilities from failure to repair or replace systems under the O&M performance warranties, while aggregate performance-guarantee caps were approximately $846.1 million and remaining potential exposure was approximately $468.9 million at June 30, 2026; payments were $5.4 million in Q2 and $13.8 million in H1. The exposure is contractual potential, not a forecast of realized cash loss, and fleet-vintage claim rates are unavailable.
realization_factors.impact: Low output or low efficiency can convert service revenue into guarantee payments, warranty work, replacement expense, and cash leakage. This factor mainly modifies service margin and cash conversion, but persistent claims can interrupt renewals and make a growing fleet economically dilutive even when reported service revenue continues to rise.

observability.match_condition: Future filings or service disclosures show guarantee claims and payments, warranty accruals, repair and replacement cost, remaining exposure, low-output or low-efficiency rates by fleet vintage, and service gross margin before and after those costs.

potential_gaps.gap_id: Aging-fleet performance remains within service assumptions
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: Across successive reporting periods, older Energy Server cohorts maintain contracted availability and output or efficiency within O&M assumptions, with degradation, downtime, and forced outages not materially increasing.
potential_gaps.derivation: Service revenue reached $69.0 million and grew 26.8% year over year with approximately 19% service gross margin, but fleet-level age cohorts, availability, efficiency, degradation, and forced-outage series are not disclosed. A multi-period cohort record would therefore provide the positive operating evidence missing from a single growing-revenue quarter.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Upgrade the availability and degradation factor and support a more durable service-life and profitability proposition. Stable operating cohorts would not by themselves prove O&M contract retention, service pricing, or cash margin after guarantees.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: Service disclosures report age-cohort availability, output or efficiency, degradation, downtime, and forced outages across at least two reporting periods, with results within the stated O&M or contractual assumptions.

potential_gaps.gap_id: Early degradation or stack failure cluster
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: An identified Energy Server fleet vintage shows materially accelerated degradation or stack/system failure, causing repeated forced outages and replacements.
potential_gaps.derivation: The current fleet condition is only moderately evidenced, while performance-guarantee payments are already active and the remaining contractual exposure is large relative to current service revenue. The missing vintage curve leaves open a failure path in which a particular generation or operating cohort ages worse than the aggregate quarter suggests.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Downgrade the proposition's availability and service-profitability support for the affected vintage, increase replacement and guarantee costs, and lengthen the time needed to validate the fleet's aging curve. Do not extrapolate the cluster to all units without cohort evidence.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: Fleet or customer reporting identifies an age or product cohort with output or availability below its service assumptions and repeated stack/system replacements or forced outages above the previously disclosed pattern.

potential_gaps.gap_id: AI duty-cycle change reveals faster fleet wear
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: High-density data-center customers operate newer Energy Server fleets at materially different utilization, cycling, thermal, or fuel conditions from legacy C&I cohorts, and those units develop a distinct availability, degradation, or maintenance profile.
potential_gaps.derivation: Bloom's current growth is increasingly tied to AI and large-load deployments, while the service evidence comes from an installed fleet whose customer mix and operating regimes are not disclosed. A change in duty cycle can expose a missing transmission step between installed MW growth and service economics even if legacy cohorts remain healthy.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Replace a single fleet-wide degradation assumption with customer- or duty-cycle-specific service expectations and revise availability, replacement timing, and service margin for the newer cohort. Customer adoption or deployment would not be treated as evidence of service profitability until the operating profile is observed.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: Operating or customer data identify a materially different utilization, cycling, thermal, or fuel regime for data-center units and show a correlated divergence in availability, degradation, repair, or replacement metrics across multiple sites.

potential_gaps.gap_id: O&M renewal and pricing sustain service capture
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: Expiring O&M contracts are renewed across a growing installed base with scope and pricing or escalators that cover ordinary labor, parts, replacements, and guarantee obligations, and service revenue per MW remains stable or rises.
potential_gaps.derivation: Bloom attributes service growth to an expanding maintenance-contract fleet, but installed MW under contract, renewal and churn rates, pricing, escalators, duration, and service revenue per MW are not disclosed. A renewal wave with adequate economics would validate the conversion of installed assets into recurring service revenue rather than merely confirm fleet growth.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Upgrade support for durable service-revenue capture and the ability to fund maintenance, replacement, and guarantee obligations from recurring contracts. The revision would not establish availability or low degradation without operating data.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: Disclosures show renewals for a material expiring cohort, the related installed MW under O&M, contract scope and pricing or escalation, and stable or improved service revenue per MW and margin after ordinary field costs.

potential_gaps.gap_id: O&M churn or self-maintenance erodes service capture
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: A material customer or fleet cohort declines to renew O&M, insources maintenance, or renegotiates service scope or pricing downward as systems age while Bloom retains warranty or performance obligations.
potential_gaps.derivation: The current shell has service revenue growth but no renewal, churn, self-maintenance, or scope-leakage history. Customers can separate service rights from installed equipment, and warranty or performance obligations can persist after commercial service revenue is reduced, creating a distinct capture failure.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Lower expected recurring service revenue and margin per installed MW and revise the proposition so fleet growth no longer implies service-profit growth. Retained warranty or guarantee work would increase the cost and cash burden of the non-renewed cohort.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: A filing or customer disclosure records material non-renewal, customer self-maintenance, termination, or price/scope reduction and also identifies continuing Bloom warranty or performance obligations for the affected systems.

potential_gaps.gap_id: Parts and technician bottleneck extends fleet downtime
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: Critical replacement parts or qualified field technicians become constrained, producing a multi-site repair backlog, longer mean time to repair, and prolonged outages.
potential_gaps.derivation: Bloom identifies field maintenance and service activity as a growing business, but the current evidence does not disclose parts lead times, technician capacity, replacement cadence, mean time to repair, or post-repair availability. Supply-chain pressure and rapid deployment can therefore migrate into the service network after installation.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Downgrade the maintenance-execution factor, increase downtime, guarantee, replacement, and service-cost assumptions, and lower confidence that service revenue converts to profit. The event would not by itself prove a product-design failure if availability recovers after capacity is restored.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: Operating data or filings report a growing repair backlog or mean time to repair together with constrained parts or technician capacity and a measurable deterioration in fleet availability or guarantee performance across multiple sites.

potential_gaps.gap_id: Standardized maintenance program restores fleet economics
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: A regional service network, predictive-maintenance program, or standardized stack/replacement process reduces mean time to repair and cost per MW across aging cohorts while post-repair availability improves.
potential_gaps.derivation: Bloom and its service partners have an economic incentive to convert the disclosed maintenance-contract growth into a repeatable field process, yet the current factor has no repair-cycle history. A visible improvement across aging cohorts would show that degradation need not translate one-for-one into persistent downtime or margin erosion.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Upgrade maintenance and replacement execution and improve the expected conversion of service revenue into availability and margin. The result would not remove the need to test long-term degradation or guarantee exposure across later cohorts.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: Repeated operating disclosures show lower mean time to repair or replacement cost per MW after a named service intervention, together with improved post-repair availability across more than one aging cohort.

potential_gaps.gap_id: Performance-guarantee claims crystallize across a fleet vintage
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: Performance-guarantee claims and cash payments materially accelerate for one or more fleet vintages, converting a meaningful portion of the disclosed potential exposure into actual credits, repairs, replacements, or payments.
potential_gaps.derivation: Bloom reported $5.4 million of Q2 and $13.8 million of H1 performance-guarantee payments and approximately $468.9 million of potential remaining exposure, while explicitly lacking fleet-vintage claim rates. A claims cluster would show that service revenue growth is being offset by economically active underperformance rather than only by ordinary maintenance.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Downgrade service gross-margin and cash-conversion expectations, increase the realized-cost portion of the guarantee exposure, and raise customer-renewal risk for the affected cohort. The remaining contractual cap would still not be treated as a forecast of total loss absent realized claims.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: A filing or service disclosure links a material increase in guarantee claims, payments, accruals, repairs, or replacements to a fleet vintage or customer cohort and reports the effect on service margin or availability.

potential_gaps.gap_id: Performance-guarantee claims remain contained
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: Subsequent fleet reporting shows declining performance-guarantee claim rates and payments per serviced MW, with remaining exposure falling for operating reasons rather than merely from portfolio runoff.
potential_gaps.derivation: The current record has active payments but no comparable per-MW, age-cohort, or post-repair series; the filing also reports no liabilities for failure to repair or replace systems under O&M performance warranties. A longitudinal containment record is a plausible positive path that would separate contractual exposure from realized service leakage.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Upgrade support for bounded warranty and guarantee costs and improve the expected durability of service margin. A lower aggregate payment caused only by fewer serviced units or contract expiry would not match; the revision requires operating or cohort-level evidence.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: At least two subsequent reporting periods disclose lower normalized guarantee claims or payments per serviced MW or per comparable cohort, with accompanying availability or efficiency evidence and a declining exposure attributable to performance improvement or resolved claims.

potential_gaps.gap_id: Remote controls or monitoring outage disrupts service
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: A cyber, software, controls, or remote-monitoring incident derates or disconnects a group of installed Energy Servers and delays diagnosis or restoration.
potential_gaps.derivation: The current model emphasizes physical degradation, parts, and guarantees, while a geographically distributed installed fleet also depends on controls, monitoring, and coordinated service response. A connected-system failure would enter from outside the present physical-aging ontology and could create correlated downtime without a preceding component replacement trend.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Add digital and control-system resilience as a required service condition and temporarily lower availability, restoration, and service-margin expectations for the affected fleet. A contained incident would revise monitoring and contingency assumptions without proving a general hardware-degradation failure.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: Bloom, a customer, or a regulator identifies a cyber, software, controls, or remote-monitoring event with multi-site Energy Server derating or outage, a documented restoration interval, and measurable repair, guarantee, or service-cost effects.

potential_gaps.gap_id: Fuel-quality or supply shock derates a regional fleet
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: A gas-quality, pressure, pipeline, or other fuel-supply interruption affects a regional Energy Server fleet and causes derating, outages, or performance-guarantee claims despite maintenance capacity being available.
potential_gaps.derivation: Energy Servers are deployed around fuel and site-infrastructure conditions, and Project Jupiter's proposed gas pipeline illustrates that fuel readiness remains an external field dependency. A regional fuel event would challenge the assumption that availability and degradation can be managed solely through equipment maintenance and would create a correlated service path outside the current age-cohort data.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Revise availability and guarantee assumptions to include fuel-quality and regional infrastructure exposure, and lower expected service profitability for affected sites until fuel is restored or systems are adapted. The event would not by itself establish a fleet-wide degradation rate.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: A utility, customer, operator, or Bloom disclosure links a regional Energy Server derating, outage, or guarantee claim to fuel quality, pressure, pipeline, or other fuel-supply conditions and records recovery or mitigation.

potential_gaps.gap_id: Fleet growth dilutes service economics through warranty or bundled support mix
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: Installed Energy Server MW grows faster than service revenue because new deployments carry bundled, low-priced, customer-managed, or warranty-only support, and service gross margin falls as field obligations accumulate.
potential_gaps.derivation: Service revenue is growing, but the current state does not disclose installed MW under O&M, contract attachment, pricing, scope, or the share of new systems still covered by warranty. A larger installed base can therefore produce less recurring service capture per MW if commercial terms or customer responsibility change as deployment scales.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Decouple installed-fleet growth from the expectation of proportional service revenue and profit, lower service revenue per MW or margin assumptions, and recognize a longer lag before the fleet becomes economically recurring. The revision concerns service capture and mix, not whether the systems are physically operating.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: Reporting discloses installed MW increasing faster than O&M-covered MW or service revenue and attributes the divergence to bundled, warranty-only, customer-managed, low-price, or otherwise reduced service scope, with a corresponding margin decline.

shells.shell_id: Corporate financial realization and per-share earnings
shells.core_question: Will Bloom's operating ramp become durable, cash-generative, and accretive per share after normalized product margins, operating expenses, working capital, capital intensity, liquidity, and capital-instrument effects are reflected?
shells.boundary_rule: This shell is the corporate financial-realization research system: management guidance and financial statements; manufacturing product margins; operating-expense leverage; earnings duration; operating cash conversion; capacity investment, capital intensity, liquidity and financing capacity; and capital instruments, share count and diluted EPS. Although it contains six distinct Units, they share the same normalized corporate-accounting and guidance context while margin, opex, duration, cash timing, investment funding and per-share effects retain different evidence cadences. Demand, permits, manufacturing capacity, field service and project execution are upstream inputs; price, valuation, multiples, options and short-interest inference are excluded, and earnings duration remains conditional on operating evidence rather than a claim about what the market has priced.

units.proposition: Bloom can sustain Energy Server product unit economics that support roughly 34% FY2026 non-GAAP company-wide gross margin and remain durable after tariff recovery, materials and logistics, price-cost, mix, quality, and manufacturing-scale effects normalize.
units.horizon: FY2026 and subsequent reporting quarters as scale and cost normalization are observed.

parameters.definition: Bloom Energy Server product gross margin for a reported fiscal quarter, calculated on the GAAP product revenue and product cost-of-revenue basis and excluding service, installation, and electricity categories.
Management's stated FY2026 non-GAAP gross-margin percentage guidance on the disclosed company-wide basis; it is not treated as a product-only GAAP margin.
Bloom Energy Server product revenue recognized in a specified fiscal reporting period, separate from installation, service, and electricity revenue.

Current evidence stance on whether Energy Server product unit economics can support the margin target after tariff recovery, materials and logistics, price-cost, mix, quality, warranty, and manufacturing-scale effects are considered.

values.state_value_id: Q2 2026 Energy Server product GAAP gross margin
FY2026 management non-GAAP gross margin guidance
FY2026 management product margin normalization evidence

realization_factors.condition: Energy Server product unit costs remain compatible with a roughly 34% FY2026 non-GAAP company-wide gross-margin outcome after tariff recovery, materials, labor, logistics, warranty, and price-cost effects are normalized.
realization_factors.current_status: At the 2026-09-21 research cutoff, Q2 Energy Server product gross margin was about 37% and management maintained roughly 34% FY2026 non-GAAP gross-margin guidance. Manufacturing and material improvements supported Q2, but the quarter also included about $37.4 million of imported-duty recovery; new tariffs, commodity prices, freight, warranty costs, and incomplete price pass-through leave recurring cost normalization mixed rather than established.
realization_factors.impact: This is the product-margin transmission from input and logistics costs to corporate gross profit. Durable automation and price recovery support operating leverage; non-recurring duty recovery, fixed-price projects, or weak pass-through can lower product margin and reduce the operating-income outcome without independently eliminating demand.

observability.match_condition: A subsequent quarterly product-cost bridge or product gross-margin disclosure shows Energy Server margin after separating tariff refunds, commodity and freight costs, warranty, and price changes; a renewed margin decline or identified recurring pass-through failure would update this factor.

realization_factors.factor_id: Manufacturing scale, yield, and quality conversion
realization_factors.condition: Fremont and Delmarva automation and capacity expansion produce qualified Energy Server units at lower repeatable cost without yield, defect, rework, or warranty deterioration.
realization_factors.current_status: At cutoff, management attributed Q2 product-margin improvement partly to process improvement, automation, and lower material, labor, and manufacturing costs, and reported no major component shortage expected to change the 2026 production outlook. The approximately 2 GW capacity objective remains a plan; effective qualified output, supplier qualification, yield, and fleet-quality history are not yet demonstrated at the required scale.
realization_factors.impact: Qualified scale is the mechanism that converts capacity investment and product demand into repeatable unit economics. If output scales with stable yield and quality, fixed manufacturing costs are absorbed; if ramp defects, supplier substitutions, or warranty and performance issues rise, rework and service obligations can offset the gross-margin benefit.

observability.match_condition: Future Fremont or Delmarva disclosures report qualified throughput, supplier qualification, yield, defect or rework rates, and warranty or performance costs alongside shipments; sustained qualified output with stable quality would confirm the gate, while ramp failures would challenge it.

realization_factors.factor_id: Energy Server product mix and recognition mix
realization_factors.condition: High-margin Energy Server product revenue remains the dominant recognized mix, and project installation, service, and electricity obligations do not shift the corporate mix toward lower-margin or loss-making categories.
realization_factors.current_status: At cutoff, Q2 product revenue was $935.4 million, about 87.8% of revenue, with product gross margin near 37%; service was about 19%, installation about negative 4%, and electricity about 31%. Direct purchase and third-party PPA/channel structures represented 99% of Q2 revenue, but project milestones, installation responsibility, and mix can vary by deployment and change reported margin.
realization_factors.impact: Product mix determines how product-level economics reach consolidated gross profit. A sustained product-heavy mix supports the margin target; a greater share of installation, service, or electricity work, or project timing that recognizes lower-margin obligations first, can reduce gross margin and delay operating leverage even if Energy Server manufacturing costs improve.

observability.match_condition: Quarterly revenue mix and category-level gross margins, together with disclosed installation responsibility and project-milestone timing, show whether Energy Server product remains the dominant profit contributor or lower-margin categories are diluting the result.

potential_gaps.gap_id: Recurring tariff-and-input pass-through failure
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: Across one or more subsequent reporting quarters, newly imposed tariffs, commodity or freight costs, labor costs, or supplier price resets rise while fixed-price Energy Server projects or customer negotiations prevent Bloom from passing the increase through.
potential_gaps.derivation: Q2 product margin was supported by manufacturing improvement but also included about $37.4 million of imported-duty recovery, and the current research describes tariff, commodity, freight, warranty, and incomplete price-pass-through exposure. A renewed cost shock or a failure to recover it is therefore a plausible route from a strong reported quarter to weaker recurring product economics.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Lower support for durable product economics and for the roughly 34% FY2026 non-GAAP gross-margin outcome, and reset the product-margin-to-operating-income bridge lower for affected quarters. A single disclosed shock would not by itself prove permanently lower unit economics; recurrence or an identified structural pass-through gap would.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: A quarterly product-cost bridge identifies a new tariff, commodity, freight, labor, or supplier burden not offset by price, or Energy Server product GAAP margin falls materially below the Q2 level of roughly 37% for two consecutive quarters with management attributing the gap to recurring costs rather than a one-time item or mix alone.

potential_gaps.gap_id: Qualified scale delivers repeatable product-cost step-down
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: Fremont and Delmarva expansion and supplier qualification produce sustained qualified Energy Server throughput with lower recurring material, labor, rework, and freight cost across several quarters.
potential_gaps.derivation: Management attributed Q2 improvement partly to process improvement, automation, and lower material, labor, and manufacturing costs, while the approximately 2 GW objective remains nominal rather than proven qualified output. If the planned scale converts into stable yield and cost absorption, a further step-down in recurring product cost is possible beyond the current moderate evidence.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Increase support for durable product unit economics and for the company-wide gross-margin guidance anchor. This would validate manufacturing conversion, not prove that consolidated margin is insulated from mix, pricing, service, installation, or electricity recognition.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: At least two successive filings disclose qualified throughput or yield and recurring product-cost or margin improvement without duty refunds, unusual credits, or mix-only explanations, while warranty and rework costs remain stable.

potential_gaps.gap_id: Ramp-quality and warranty failure
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: A rapid production ramp produces abnormal defect, rework, field-failure, warranty, recall, or performance-guarantee charges in newly delivered Energy Server cohorts.
potential_gaps.derivation: Qualified output, supplier qualification, yield, and fleet-quality history have not yet been demonstrated at the planned scale, while current research already identifies warranty and performance-guarantee exposure. A scale-up can therefore reveal quality costs that were not visible in the initial margin improvement and can transmit back into product cost.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Reduce confidence that the observed product margin is durable and lower the expected product-cost and operating-income outcome for affected cohorts. If the charge is isolated and corrected, revise the timing and risk of normalization rather than permanently abandoning the margin proposition.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: Bloom discloses a material defect, rework, recall, warranty reserve, replacement, or performance-guarantee charge tied to new production cohorts together with product-cost or margin deterioration in the same or following quarters.

potential_gaps.gap_id: Lower-margin project-recognition mix
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: As large-load deployments mature, a larger share of recognized revenue comes from installation, service, electricity, or other lower-margin obligations before high-margin Energy Server product revenue is recognized.
potential_gaps.derivation: Q2 product revenue was dominant, but installation was loss-making, service and electricity had different margins, and project milestones and installation responsibility vary by contract and delivery model. A future recognition sequence can therefore dilute consolidated economics even if factory product cost remains controlled.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Lower the expected consolidated and product-led margin conversion and delay the operating-leverage implication, while preserving the possibility that underlying Energy Server manufacturing economics remain sound. The revision concerns mix and recognition, not automatic failure of the product-cost target.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: Two or more subsequent quarters show product share materially below the Q2 mix or installation, electricity, or service gross profit diluting the consolidated product-led margin, with the change linked to project or contract recognition rather than only a one-time accounting item.

potential_gaps.gap_id: Competitive price compression
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: Customers or channel partners obtain lower Energy Server prices, discounts, or more onerous performance guarantees as grid upgrades, gas turbines, storage, engines, or other firm-power alternatives become more available.
potential_gaps.derivation: The product-margin factor depends on price-cost as well as manufacturing cost, and the industry research describes both a near-term time-to-power opportunity and expanding alternative firm-power supply. Even with strong demand, customer bargaining power can transfer part of the scarcity benefit away from Bloom.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Lower the realized-price and product-margin assumption and revise the conversion from demand to gross profit. Continued orders would not by themselves disprove the gap because the issue is value capture and unit economics rather than demand volume.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: New-order or contract disclosures identify pricing concessions, discounts, expanded guarantees, or lower realized economics while input costs are unchanged or rising, or product margin falls with management attributing the change to price or competitive mix.

potential_gaps.gap_id: Supply-chain interruption and expedited-cost shock
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: A single-source or long-lead component qualification failure, geopolitical or trade disruption, or supplier outage interrupts production and forces expensive substitutions, expediting, or air freight.
potential_gaps.derivation: Bloom is qualifying multiple suppliers and carrying inventory to manage lead times, but its solid-oxide products use specialized materials and components and remain exposed to logistics and trade conditions. A disruption can create a distinct cost path even when average input prices and demand are unchanged.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Lower near-term product-margin and earnings expectations and extend the time needed to establish normalized economics. If the disruption is temporary and costs are recovered, retain the long-run proposition but revise the path and volatility.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: Bloom reports a supplier disruption, substitution, qualification failure, or expedited-logistics response and identifies related product-cost, delivery, or margin impact in a subsequent filing.

units.expectation_id: Operating expense leverage and operating income
units.proposition: Revenue growth can outpace expansion, R&D, certification, and regulatory-support spending to produce durable operating leverage and non-GAAP operating income.
units.horizon: FY2026 through the next several fiscal years.

parameters.definition: Bloom's consolidated GAAP operating income or loss for a specified fiscal reporting period, in U.S. dollars.
Management's fully stated FY2026 non-GAAP operating-income guidance range in U.S. dollars.
Approximate FY2026 non-GAAP operating-expense percentage implied by management's guidance presentation at the midpoint, on the disclosed non-GAAP basis.
Bloom's consolidated operating expenses for a specified fiscal quarter under the reported GAAP presentation, in U.S. dollars.
Current evidence stance on whether revenue and gross-profit growth are outpacing expansion, R&D, certification, and regulatory-support spending on a durable basis.

values.state_value_id: FY2026 management non-GAAP operating income guidance
FY2026 approximate management non-GAAP operating expense ratio

realization_factors.condition: Growth in product gross profit and revenue continues to outpace expansion, engineering, R&D, certification, and regulatory-support spending required to win and deliver projects.
realization_factors.current_status: At cutoff, Q2 GAAP operating income was $182 million versus a prior-year operating loss, while operating expenses were $173.3 million and up 56.7% year over year, driven in part by employee compensation and AI-data-center engineering, certification, and regulatory support. Management raised FY2026 non-GAAP operating-income guidance to $800–900 million and implied roughly a 13% non-GAAP operating-expense ratio, but multi-quarter leverage is not established.
realization_factors.impact: This is the central conversion from gross-profit growth to operating income. Scale can absorb capability-building costs, but if project qualification, regulatory support, hiring, or expansion costs rise with each deployment, revenue growth will not produce durable operating leverage and the guidance outcome will be delayed or reduced.

observability.match_condition: Subsequent quarters show revenue and gross-profit growth, GAAP and non-GAAP operating expenses, and operating income; operating leverage is confirmed when expense growth remains below gross-profit growth without a comparable reduction in required project capability.

realization_factors.condition: The costs excluded or normalized in non-GAAP operating income, including recurring compensation and other project-enablement items, do not mask a persistent economic operating burden.
realization_factors.current_status: At cutoff, management guidance is on a non-GAAP basis and the available research does not provide a reliable, stable GAAP reconciliation; Q2 operating expense growth included compensation and growth-enablement costs. The non-GAAP target is therefore directionally supported by the reported turn to operating profit, but the normalized recurring expense base remains only moderately evidenced.
realization_factors.impact: Adjustment quality changes the magnitude and comparability of operating leverage. If excluded costs are recurring, non-GAAP operating income can overstate the durable corporate contribution; if they are genuinely nonrecurring and capability converts into revenue, the reported leverage can persist.

observability.match_condition: Future filings or guidance provide a period-by-period GAAP-to-non-GAAP operating-income bridge and identify recurring stock compensation, certification, regulatory, and other adjustments; stable exclusions with continued GAAP improvement support the factor, while recurring exclusions weaken it.

potential_gaps.gap_id: Multi-quarter operating leverage confirmation
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: Revenue and product gross profit continue to grow across successive quarters while expansion, engineering, certification, regulatory-support, and corporate operating expenses grow more slowly on both GAAP and comparable non-GAAP bases.
potential_gaps.derivation: Q2 GAAP operating income turned positive and management raised FY2026 non-GAAP operating-income guidance, but expenses still grew materially with AI-data-center support. A repeated conversion of gross profit into operating income would establish a stronger mechanism than the single-quarter observation.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Increase confidence in durable operating leverage, support the FY2026 operating-income range, and extend the earnings-base expectation beyond the first profitable quarter. The evidence would not by itself settle product margin, cash conversion, or diluted EPS.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: At least three consecutive reporting quarters show gross-profit growth exceeding comparable operating-expense growth, positive operating income, and no comparable reduction in required project, certification, or regulatory capability.

potential_gaps.gap_id: Project-support costs outrun gross-profit growth
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: Engineering, certification, permitting, regulatory support, field enablement, hiring, or customer-specific integration costs grow faster than gross profit as large-load deployments expand.
potential_gaps.derivation: Q2 operating expenses rose 56.7% year over year and management attributed part of the increase to AI-data-center engineering, certification, and regulatory support. A larger or more complex project pipeline can make these costs variable with each deployment rather than absorbed by scale.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Lower confidence in the 13%-style operating-expense ratio and reduce or defer the non-GAAP operating-income expectation. Revenue growth would remain possible, but the corporate conversion from growth to operating profit would be weaker and slower.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: Two or more quarters show operating-expense growth at or above gross-profit growth, with management or filings linking the increase to recurring project qualification, engineering, certification, regulatory, or customer-support requirements.

potential_gaps.gap_id: Recurring exclusions revealed in the non-GAAP bridge
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: Future filings disclose that stock compensation, retention, certification, regulatory, restructuring, or other items excluded from non-GAAP operating income recur at a material level as the business scales.
potential_gaps.derivation: The current guidance is on a non-GAAP basis and the available research does not provide a stable GAAP reconciliation, while Q2 expense growth included compensation and growth-enablement costs. A fuller bridge could show that reported non-GAAP leverage overstates the economic operating burden.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Lower durable operating-income quality and revise the normalized operating-income proposition lower if the costs recur. Headline non-GAAP guidance would no longer be sufficient evidence of leverage; genuinely finite, one-time items would instead change comparability and timing.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: A period-by-period GAAP-to-non-GAAP bridge shows the same excluded categories recurring across at least two reporting periods or rising with deployment volume, without a credible finite end point.

potential_gaps.gap_id: Compliance, safety, litigation, or recall cost shock
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: A product-safety, environmental, regulatory, litigation, or disclosure event causes Bloom to add a material operating workforce, investigation, legal reserve, remediation program, or customer-support burden.
potential_gaps.derivation: The current operating model emphasizes project engineering and regulatory support but does not assume a discrete model-breaking event. A rapidly scaling, regulated power platform can encounter a compliance or liability development that adds operating cost independently of revenue growth.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Lower near-term operating income and delay the point at which operating leverage is considered durable. If the charge is one-time and remediation reduces future risk, revise duration and comparability rather than treating the event as permanent opex inflation.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: Bloom or a regulator discloses a material investigation, recall, remediation, litigation reserve, compliance program, or customer-support cost recognized in operating expense and linked to the Energy Server business.

potential_gaps.gap_id: Strategic capability build resets the expense base
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: Bloom commits to a major new product, software, service, international, carbon-management, or manufacturing capability and materially increases engineering, sales, or corporate headcount before associated revenue arrives.
potential_gaps.derivation: Management is investing in AI-data-center qualification and production scale while the platform spans Energy Server, service, and other applications. A strategic decision to internalize more capability or pursue a new market could be rational but temporarily reverse the assumed expense absorption.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Move the operating-leverage horizon later and lower the interim operating-income margin, while preserving an upside path if the new capability later produces incremental gross profit. The occurrence would revise timing and investment intensity, not necessarily demand.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: Management announces a program with a material recurring headcount, R&D, sales, facility, or certification commitment and subsequent filings show the related operating expense rising before corresponding revenue or gross profit is reported.

potential_gaps.gap_id: Channelized delivery lowers recurring operating burden
potential_gaps.possible_occurrence: Certified installers, utility channels, financing partners, or standardized deployment systems absorb more qualification, sales, installation-support, or project-management work, reducing Bloom's recurring operating cost per deployment.
potential_gaps.derivation: Bloom is developing channel and financing relationships and has described third-party installation and consult-only delivery models. If those arrangements become operational rather than merely available, fixed corporate support costs could be absorbed or avoided earlier than the current evidence implies.
potential_gaps.expected_revision: Increase confidence in earlier operating leverage and improve the expected conversion of project growth into operating income. The revision is limited to operating expense and delivery-support burden; channel fees, margin sharing, and customer acceptance still constrain the result.
potential_gaps.recognition_criteria: Subsequent disclosures show repeated projects using third-party or channel delivery with lower Bloom project-support expense per unit or lower operating-expense growth, without simply shifting the same costs into another excluded category.

units.horizon: FY2026 through subsequent multi-year earnings periods.
